reigns.note: In Eumelus' Corinthian History, as Pausanias reports it, Helius gave Ephyraea to Aeetes; when Aeetes departed for Colchis he left the land in trust — the Colchian king first holding the site later called Corinth.
Son of Hermes and Alcidamea; entrusted with Ephyraea when Aeetes left for Colchis, and founder of the temple of Hera Bunaea on the Acrocorinthus.

Son of Marathon (son of Epopeus) in Eumelus; eponym of the land after Ephyraea was renamed. Died childless — the Corinthians then sent for Medea from Iolcus. Local speech also called him a son of Zeus, which Pausanias treats as unserious.

Pausanias' Eumelus strand: the Corinthians bestowed the kingdom on Medea after Corinthus died childless, and through her Jason was king. She later departed and handed the throne to Sisyphus — a chronology that rivals Apollodorus' Creon-era Medea at Corinth.

Craftiest of men: Apollodorus and Homer make him founder-dweller of Ephyra (later Corinth); Pausanias has Medea hand him the kingdom when she leaves. Father of Glaucus, Ornytion, Thersander, and Almus.
Son of Sisyphus and father of Bellerophon in the Homeric Aeolid stem — not the Lycian Glaucus of the Trojan War. Pausanias' continuous Corinthian roll continues instead through Ornytion's son Thoas.
Younger son of Ornytion son of Sisyphus; remained at Corinth when his brother Phocus migrated to Tithorea. Not the Lemnian Thoas, the Taurian king, or any other homonym.
Son of Thoas in Pausanias' Ornytionid succession — not the later Messenian sculptor Damophon.
Son of Damophon; father of the last Aeolid twin-kings before the Dorian takeover.
Sons of Propodas; while they were kings the Dorians under Aletes took Corinth — they gave up the kingship but remained in the city as the people were expelled.

Heraclid son of Hippotas who led the Dorians against Corinth and received the kingship from Doridas and Hyanthidas. His line ran five generations to Bacchis; not Aletes son of Aegisthus nor the Lacedaemonian son of Icarius.

King of Corinth in the Oedipus saga — his neatherds found the exposed infant on Cithaeron. Not in Pausanias' Corinthian king catalogue (and distinct from Polybus of Sicyon at Paus. 2.6.6); listed after the Pausanias roll because relative place beside the Ornytionids is unattested.

King of Corinth in Apollodorus' Jason–Medea episode — distinct from Creon of Thebes (`creon`). Betrothed Glauce to Jason and perished in Medea's poisoned robe. Hyginus wrongly calls him son of Menoeceus. Rivals Pausanias' earlier Medea–Jason kingship; not in Pausanias' continuous roll.
